clue.text: Poet's written about the biker's habits

indicators.note: the poet's name is written around the other piece, so it encloses it

parts.note: Edward Lear, the nonsense poet, with the possessive S
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet has composed verses describing a biker's usual practices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habits' looks like customs, but here it means clothing, as a monk's habit does; 'written about' signals one piece enclosing the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Motorcyclists wear protective suits of hide, so their clothing or garb is this.

clue.text: Rise in morale when English airmen enter rescue boat

indicators.note: enter means go inside, so the airmen's letters go into the morale boost

parts.note: a lift is a boost to the spirits
the RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force

explanation.surface: Morale rises when English pilots climb into a lifeboat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise in morale' reads as part of the story but is the container; 'enter' signals the airmen and English going inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflatable craft carried for emergencies at sea saves people when a ship sinks.

clue.text: Pilot coming from Yugoslavia to Russia

indicators.note: coming from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A flyer arrives from Yugoslavia on the way to Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: The run spans the end of Yugoslavia, all of 'to' and the R of Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who flies an aircraft is an airman.

clue.text: Strong, well-built sled dog

explanation.surface: Describing a sturdy dog that pulls sledges.
explanation.definitionFit: Burly and brawny is one sense; an Arctic breed of draught dog is the other.

clue.text: Something worn by equestrian, as was the custom in Yorkshire?

definitions.text: as was the custom in Yorkshire?

explanation.surface: A horsewoman's outfit linked to old Yorkshire tradition.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire was historically divided into three Ridings; a custom there would be a Riding habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's outfit for horseback is one sense; jokingly, a practice of a Yorkshire division is the other.

clue.text: What a surfer needs on boat?

explanation.surface: A riddle about equipment a surfer must take out on a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as A BOARD, it is the surfer's kit; as one word it means on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A surfer must have a single plank to ride; being on a ship is being on deck or on board.

clue.text: Violently attacks centre of sleazy London area

parts.note: batters means beats violently

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters

explanation.surface: Thugs attack the seedy heart of a district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Battersea is a district of south London on the Thames, known for its power station and dogs' home.
explanation.definitionFit: A district of south-west London beside the Thames.

clue.text: Greek maiden, note, coming after husband in a contest

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in places the husband-and-note pair inside the contest

parts.note: a race is a contest of speed

indicators.note: coming after means the note follows the husband

parts.note: n. is the abbreviation for a note, as in footnotes

explanation.surface: A Greek girl and a married man compete in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts H then N inside RACE, after A. In myth Arachne challenged Athena to weaving and was turned into a spider.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth she was a young Lydian weaver changed into a spider by Athena.

clue.text: Ultimately, parched soil could result in famine

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the next word

parts.note: earth is soil

explanation.surface: Dry ground could eventually lead to starvation.
explanation.walkthrough: D, the last letter of 'parched', joins EARTH.
explanation.definitionFit: A scarcity or lack, especially of food, is a severe shortage.

clue.text: Team showing disrespect? For the record, that's fairly unimportant

definitions.text: For the record, that's fairly unimportant

parts.note: flip means flippant, cheekily disrespectful
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A rude team is reprimanded, then the remark is dismissed as trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the record' points to vinyl singles: the reverse of a single carried the lesser track, and figuratively the term means the less important aspect.
explanation.definitionFit: On an old single, the B-side carried the minor track, so the reverse of a record is the less significant part.

clue.text: Old inventor retiring to a city in Canada

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the inventor's name is read backwards

parts.note: James Watt, Scottish inventor of steam-engine improvements
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly inventor moves to a Canadian city to retire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' signals going backwards, so the inventor's name is reversed to TTAW.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the capital of the Canadian federation, in Ontario.

clue.text: How the hoodwinked Pied Piper felt, when Hamelin no longer was?

definitions.text: How the hoodwinked Pied Piper felt

explanation.surface: The cheated Pied Piper's mood once he had cleared Hamelin of vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: The town refused to pay the Piper after he lured its rodents away: he was irritable, and the town was no longer infested.
explanation.definitionFit: Irritable and tetchy describes the unpaid Piper; overrun with rodents describes Hamelin before he came.

clue.text: Shuts nine rebels in military shelter

indicators.note: rebels as a verb means rises up, so these letters break out of their order

explanation.surface: A mutiny by nine soldiers is shut down in an army hut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rebels' is a verb signalling a shake-up of SHUTS NINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A prefabricated corrugated-iron hut of semicircular section, used by troops in the World Wars.

clue.text: Way I write journal, receiving regular payment

parts.note: ST is street, a way
to pen is to write
a diary is a daily journal

explanation.surface: Explaining how someone keeps a journal while on a salary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' is the usual crossword street abbreviation; 'write' is a verb giving a writing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Paid a fixed salary or allowance, as a magistrate or clergyman on a stipend.

clue.text: Push to get decision in favour of including article in church magazine

parts.note: for means supporting, in favour of

indicators.note: including means the church-magazine pieces hold the article inside them

parts.note: CE is the Church of England abbreviation
an issue is a single edition of a magazine
the definite article in grammar

explanation.surface: Someone pushes a church magazine to rule on including a particular item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Including' places the article inside the church magazine; 'Push to get decision' is the definition, not a story about a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: To compel a matter to be settled now is to make the question come to a head.

clue.text: Extended access in east London? That's not on

indicators.note: in puts the access inside the shortened city
not on says the letters O and N are dropped from the city name

parts.note: the capital, written in full
a gate gives access

explanation.surface: Someone protests that extended entry into east London is unacceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East London' suggests the East End, but east and London are separate pieces; 'That's not on' removes ON, leaving LOND, and 'in' puts access inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Lengthened or stretched out means made longer.

clue.text: Alienate sergeant in mess

indicators.note: in a mess means jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sergeant upsets colleagues in the mess hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' looks like the soldiers' dining room, but 'in mess' signals a jumble of SERGEANT.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone unfriendly or distant is to drive them away.

clue.text: Leader of the Moscow mint employees who could cause problems?

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: workers at a Russian mint would produce roubles, the Russian currency

explanation.surface: The head of Moscow's mint staff are suspected of stirring up unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: T, the first letter of 'the', joins people who make roubles at the Russian mint.
explanation.definitionFit: People who stir up strife or agitation are those causing problems.

clue.text: Convict wearing hat cultivated land

indicators.note: wearing means the hat goes round the convict

parts.note: tile is slang for a hat
a lag is a convict, as in old lag

explanation.surface: A prisoner in a hat works the fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' signals the hat going round the convict. A tile is old British slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Ploughed and tilled ground is farmland under the plough.

clue.text: European cause arousing strong feeling

parts.note: a motive is a reason or cause

explanation.surface: A European cause that stirs up passion.
explanation.definitionFit: Stirring the emotions describes something charged with emotion.

clue.text: -So sad, wandering round European port

indicators.note: round means the rearranged letters surround the European
wandering means the letters stray from their order

explanation.surface: Someone sorrowfully drifts about a European harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering' mixes SO SAD into ODSSA; 'round' puts E inside after D.
explanation.definitionFit: A major Ukrainian harbour city on the Black Sea.

clue.text: Pleased to be plunged into darkness?

explanation.surface: A riddle about being happy when the lights go out.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as DE-LIGHTED, the word means with the light taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Happy and thrilled is one sense; jokingly, having one's illumination removed is the other.

clue.text: Bertie's no saint: he's going courting

indicators.note: no here means without, so the saint's letters are dropped

parts.note: Bertie Wooster, P G Wodehouse's comic hero

explanation.surface: Wodehouse's Bertie is no angel as he goes chasing after a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Bertie Wooster is the amiable idler of P G Wodehouse's Jeeves stories; 'no' removes ST from his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A suitor who pursues romance and seeks to win a partner is a courting man.

clue.text: Mad Liverpool friend seen with nothing on

parts.note: wack is Scouse (Liverpool) slang for a pal
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A crazy Liverpudlian mate is seen naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wack' is Liverpool dialect for mate, a form of address; 'on' sets O after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy or eccentric is slang for insane.

clue.text: Song sung by sailors in hut

explanation.surface: Sailors singing a work song inside a shack.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea song sung while hauling is one sense; a crude shack or shed is the other.

clue.text: Approve penalty for disobeying law

explanation.surface: Agreeing to a punishment for those who break the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to authorise and a punitive measure imposed for breach, a contronym.

clue.text: After a long time, lawyer introduces new list of items to be addressed

definitions.text: list of items to be addressed

indicators.note: introduces means comes in front of, so new is placed before the lawyer

parts.note: an age is a very long period
DA is a US district attorney, a prosecuting lawyer

explanation.surface: After a long delay, a lawyer brings in a new schedule of business for the meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After a long time' puts that piece first; 'introduces' means new comes in front of the lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: A meeting's schedule of business to be discussed is its programme.

clue.text: Novice shelters, say, a mountain dweller

parts.note: a tyro is a beginner or novice

indicators.note: say indicates the next word is heard as it is spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: lees are places sheltered from the wind

explanation.surface: A beginner protects, for example, someone living high up in the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' makes LEES heard, written LESE. The Tyrol is an Alpine region of Austria and Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the Tyrol, an Alpine region, is a native of mountain country.
